title: Reformation: one Confederation, two faiths
card: From Zwingli's Zurich to the Peace of Aarau: how each place in Switzerland became Reformed, Catholic or both, and why it led to four wars.

stops.title: Zwingli changes Zurich
text: On 1 January 1519 Huldrych Zwingli starts as priest at the Grossmünster in Zurich. He teaches that only the Bible is the rule for faith. In 1522 friends of Zwingli eat sausages in Lent, which the Church forbids. This becomes a public dispute.

The city council supports Zwingli against the bishop of Constance. After public debates (disputations) in 1523, the council removes the images from the churches in June 1524 and takes over the monasteries in December. In April 1525 Zurich stops the Catholic Mass.

The five inner cantons (Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug) promise in 1524 to keep the old faith. In Appenzell, the Landsgemeinde (assembly of all men) decides in 1525 that each parish chooses its own faith.

stops.title: Bern joins the Reformation
text: In January 1528 Bern holds a large public debate. A few days later the council decides to introduce the Reformation. Bern is a powerful city-state, so this decision is a turning point.

Bern brings the Reformation into its lands, by force where needed. In the Hasli valley about half of the people rebel, but Bern stops the revolt. Biel also becomes Reformed in 1528. The French preacher Guillaume Farel works in Aigle, a Bernese land.

In the east the town of St. Gallen under Vadian is already Reformed, and the Toggenburg follows. In Thurgau a Landsgemeinde declares freedom of faith in December 1528. In Graubünden the Ilanz Articles (1524, 1526) let each commune choose its pastor.

stops.title: Basel, Schaffhausen, First Kappel War
text: In 1529 Basel (February) and Schaffhausen also become Reformed. In Glarus the Landsgemeinde lets each commune decide. The Reformed towns make an alliance (Christian Burgrecht); the five Catholic cantons ally with King Ferdinand of Habsburg.

Schwyz burns the Reformed pastor Jakob Kaiser. Zurich declares war on 8 June 1529 and marches to Kappel on the Zug border. Neutral cantons find a compromise, and there is no battle. The story says that soldiers from both sides ate milk soup together.

The First Land Peace (26 June 1529) helps the Reformed side. In the common lordships (lands ruled together by several cantons) each parish now decides by majority. Many parishes in Thurgau, Rheintal, the Freie Ämter and the abbot's lands turn Reformed.

stops.title: Second Kappel War
text: Zurich wants Reformed preaching in the five inner cantons too. In May 1531 Zurich and Bern stop the sale of grain and salt to them. The five cantons answer with war. On 11 October 1531 they defeat Zurich at Kappel. Zwingli dies in the battle. A second Catholic victory follows at the Gubel in the night of 23 to 24 October.

The Second Land Peace (20 November 1531) fixes faith by place: each canton keeps its own faith. In the common lordships, parishes may go back to the Catholic faith, but not the other way. The Freie Ämter, Bremgarten and Mellingen become Catholic again at once; so do Sargans and most of the abbot's lands.

Thurgau, the Rheintal and the County of Baden get mixed parishes, often with one church for both faiths. Solothurn decides for the Catholic side in 1532. This map shows the order that lasts, with small changes, until 1712.

stops.title: Farel, Vaud and Geneva
text: After 1531 the Reformation grows in the west. Guillaume Farel preaches in French-speaking lands with Bern's support. Neuchâtel becomes Reformed in 1530; only Le Landeron and Cressier stay Catholic.

Geneva has fought for its freedom from Savoy and its bishop. On 21 May 1536 it introduces the Reformation. In the same year Bern conquers Vaud from Savoy. After a debate in Lausanne in October 1536, Bern orders the Reformation in all of Vaud.
In the lands that Bern and Fribourg rule together (Orbe, Echallens, Grandson) each parish votes on the Mass. Echallens never gives up the Mass.

stops.title: Calvin's Geneva
text: The French lawyer John Calvin flees France. In 1536 he comes to Geneva, and Farel asks him to stay. The council does not support them, and in 1538 both must leave. Calvin works in Strasbourg with Martin Bucer.

At the council's request Calvin comes back in September 1541. In November the council accepts his church order (Ordonnances ecclésiastiques). Pastors and a church court (consistory) teach and control how people live.

Bern rules Vaud and, until 1564, lands south and west of the lake (Chablais, Gex). In 1549 Zurich and Geneva agree on the Lord's Supper (Consensus Tigurinus). This joins the Zwingli and Calvin lines into one Reformed church family.

stops.title: The Swiss Reformation in Europe
text: The Reformation starts in 1517 with Martin Luther in Wittenberg. Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva start a second line, the Reformed churches. Martin Bucer of Strasbourg also shapes these churches.

In 1559 Geneva opens its Academy, a school for pastors from all of Europe. In the 1550s about 30 printers in Geneva print Reformed books, many for France. Reformed churches grow in France, the Netherlands, Scotland, Hungary and Poland. In 1559 the French Reformed churches hold their first national synod in Paris.
The Peace of Augsburg (1555) protects only Lutherans in the Empire, not the Reformed. The map shows Europe about 1560 only roughly: German states and whole countries are coloured as one.

stops.title: Catholic reform, Golden League
text: After the Council of Trent (1545–1563) the Catholic Church reforms itself. Cardinal Charles Borromeo, archbishop of Milan, is protector of the Swiss Catholics. In 1579 his Collegium Helveticum in Milan opens to train Swiss priests.

Jesuits open colleges in Lucerne (1577) and Fribourg (1582); Petrus Canisius comes to Fribourg in 1580. Capuchin friars settle in Altdorf (1581) and many other towns. From 1586 a papal envoy (nuncio) lives in Lucerne.

On 5 October 1586 the seven Catholic cantons sign the Golden League in Lucerne. They promise to keep the Catholic faith and to help each other. The bishop of Basel brings Laufen and Birseck back to the Catholic faith. Bern now rules the Pays-d'Enhaut (1555), which becomes Reformed.

stops.title: Appenzell splits in two
text: Since 1525 Appenzell has two faiths: the outer parishes are Reformed, the inner parishes Catholic. After 1580 the conflict grows, for example about a Catholic alliance with Spain.

In 1597 the land splits. Catholic Innerrhoden has its seat in Appenzell; Reformed Ausserrhoden meets in Trogen and Hundwil. Each half has its own Landsgemeinde. Innerrhoden joins the Golden League in 1600.
Glarus does not split. Its Catholics and Reformed share some offices and the church in Glarus. From 1623 each side holds its own Landsgemeinde, and there is also a common one.

stops.title: Graubünden: faith by commune
text: In the Three Leagues there is no ruler who decides the faith. Since the Ilanz Articles (1524, 1526) each commune elects its pastor and so chooses its faith. Chur turns Reformed by 1527; by about 1530 many communes of the Ten Jurisdictions, the Heinzenberg and the Schams follow. The Engadine follows after 1550.

In the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) Graubünden is fought over by Spain, Austria and France. In July 1620 Catholics in the Valtellina kill about 600 Reformed. Austrian troops try to make the Prättigau and the Lower Engadine Catholic again, without success.

By about 1640 the map is fixed and stays almost the same until 1803. The Surselva, the Oberhalbstein and the Misox are Catholic. Some communes have both faiths, for example Poschiavo, Brusio, the Vier Dörfer near Chur and Val Müstair.

stops.title: First Villmergen War
text: In Arth (Schwyz) some families secretly keep the Reformed faith. In September 1655 a group flees to Zurich. Schwyz executes four Reformed who stay. Zurich and Bern declare war on 6 January 1656.

Zurich besieges Rapperswil but cannot take it. On 24 January 1656 troops from Lucerne and Zug surprise the Bernese army at Villmergen and win. The Reformed plan to take the Freie Ämter, which separate Zurich from Bern, fails.
The Third Land Peace (7 March 1656) restores the old order of 1531. Each canton stays master of the faith in its own land. The Catholic cantons keep their lead in the common lordships.

stops.title: Villmergen and the Peace of Aarau
text: The Toggenburg, mostly Reformed, rises against its lord, the Catholic abbot of St. Gallen. Zurich and Bern support the Toggenburg; the five inner cantons support the abbot. In 1712 Zurich and Bern occupy Thurgau, take Wil and win near Bremgarten on 26 May.
On 25 July 1712 the Bernese defeat the inner cantons at Villmergen. More than 3000 men die. The Fourth Land Peace, signed in Aarau on 11 August 1712, ends the war.

Both faiths are now equal in the common lordships, with clear rules for shared churches. The Catholic cantons lose their part in the County of Baden and the lower Freie Ämter; Bern joins the rule of Thurgau, the Rheintal, Sargans and the upper Freie Ämter. The map of faiths stays, but the Catholic lead ends.

notes: Areas are today's municipalities; many were merged, so one old village with another faith can colour a whole new municipality 'mixed' (e.g. Ilanz/Glion, Domleschg, Cazis, Breil/Brigels, Obersaxen Mundaun, Scuol shown Reformed although Tarasp was Catholic and Austrian). Graubünden communes follow the Atlas Graubünden map 'Konfessionsverhältnisse um 1640' read by eye; the exact commune shown mixed near Laax/Falera was not identified (both drawn Catholic); Trimmis drawn mixed. Thurgau, Rheintal and Glarus are drawn mixed as a whole (Thurgau was mostly Reformed, with 27 shared churches); only Oberriet is singled out as Catholic in the Rheintal. Toggenburg: the upper part was mostly Reformed, the lower part mostly Catholic; the split by municipality (incl. Oberuzwil, Uzwil, Degersheim, Jonschwil) is an estimate. County of Baden: Zurzach, Würenlos, Dietikon as shared and Tegerfelden, Schlieren, Oetwil, Hüttikon as Reformed are from general knowledge, not checked one by one. 1529 step: extent of Reformed parishes in common lordships and abbey lands is approximate; Gaster/Weesen shown Reformed because they joined Zurich's 1531 blockade. Echallens group: Villars-le-Terroir, Bottens, Assens according to the source; Poliez-Pittet and Saint-Barthélemy assumed. Date for Orbe and Grandson becoming Reformed (here 1554) not checked. Laufen/Birseck: re-Catholicisation by bishop Blarer in the 1580s, drawn Catholic from 1597. Gex: rough (Bernese 1536–1564, tolerated Reformed later, Catholic by 1685). Nuncio in Lucerne 'from 1586' and Calvin's arrival month (June 1536) may differ in other sources. The Villmergen memorial is used for both battles. Europe step is very rough (whole countries, German federal states).
